lines.text: Do you know how bees make honey? It starts as flower juice, and ends up as something that almost never goes bad.
A worker bee sucks up nectar, a sugary liquid inside flowers, and carries it in a special honey stomach.
On the way home, enzymes in that stomach start breaking the sugar into simpler sugars.
In the hive, bees pass the nectar mouth to mouth, adding more enzymes each time.
Then they spread it in wax cells and fan it with their wings, drying it from around seventy percent water to under twenty.
When it's thick enough, they seal each cell with a lid of wax.
One bee makes only about a twelfth of a teaspoon in her whole life. A single jar takes thousands of bees, and millions of flowers.
And honey is so dry and acidic that germs can't grow in it. That's why it keeps for so long.
